title: Voice cloning attacks on family and finance
body_md:
## The call that begins “it’s me”

Your phone lights up at two in the morning with a number you don’t know. It is your daughter’s voice, thin and quick, saying she has been in an accident and needs money before anyone can be told.

Voice cloning can make a caller sound like somebody you know. The FTC warns that a short clip of audio from online material can be enough for a scammer to try it. That is not a rule about seconds, since tools differ, and it does not mean every convincing impersonation used AI. Caller ID can be spoofed, a real phone can be stolen, and a frightened relative can sound unlike themselves without any deception at all.

### The family emergency

The script joins a familiar voice to urgency, secrecy and a payment method that is hard to recover. The caller may bring in a second voice who claims to be a lawyer or an official. Questioning that person on the same call is not an independent check. End the call, dial your relative on a number you saved earlier, and try another close person if there is no answer. If there may be a real emergency, call the local emergency service on its established number. Do not delay care just to finish a fraud test.

### The same voice at work

A voice that sounds like an executive may ask for a confidential transfer or a change to a supplier’s details. The voice changes nothing about who has to approve a payment. Use the approved directory, the payment-change procedure and the second sign-off. A corporate chat account can be compromised too, so ask the exact person about the exact amount through a known channel, and do not read a green “online” dot as proof.

### A spare key under the flowerpot

A family phrase can be a useful extra cue if everyone understands the rule. Treat it as a spare key under the flowerpot: handy, and **not a master key**. It can be overheard, phished, forgotten under stress, or repeated by an attacker after one relative lets it slip. A childhood fact that can be found online is no better as the only test. Whether the phrase is missing or correct, still make the independent callback before sending money. And never read a one-time account code to a caller.

If money has already gone, contact your bank or payment provider promptly and ask what recovery is possible. Success is not guaranteed. Report it through the routes your country provides. The habit that holds up best is to verify the request itself, outside the call, whether or not the voice was cloned.

widget_config.goal: Verify urgent family and finance calls without leaning on a familiar voice.
widget_config.today_action: Save the independently verified number of one close person you would call in a family emergency.
widget_config.scope: General guidance. The FTC examples and reporting routes apply to the US and were checked 20 October 2026. Use your local emergency and workplace procedures. The cases and the exercise below are invented.

sources.title: FTC: Scammers Use Fake Emergencies To Steal Your Money
sources.scope: US consumer advice, September 2023: voice cloning, urgency, an independent callback and contacting another relative. The reporting route it names applies to the US only.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: US guidance on transfer and account-change requests: verify through a second channel, and contact the bank urgently after a suspected transfer. Organisational and national procedures vary.

blocks.title: A nephew in trouble asks you to tell no one
blocks.situation: A caller sounds like your nephew and says an intermediary will take a payment right away. He begs you not to contact his parents.
blocks.analysis: Secrecy and an urgent payment are the two things that stop you checking. End the call, ring your nephew on the number you saved, then reach his parents if you need to. A second voice introduced by the caller is still inside the same untrusted conversation.

blocks.title: A real emergency, an unfamiliar voice
blocks.situation: Your sister calls from a borrowed phone after a traffic accident, and the noise and panic make her voice hard to recognise. She asks you to come to a hospital, not to send money.
blocks.analysis: A strange-sounding voice is not proof of fraud. Ask for the hospital’s name, call its published switchboard or the local emergency service if you must, and act on welfare information you have confirmed. Do not demand a code phrase before offering real help.

blocks.title: A call after midnight
blocks.setup: An invented scenario: a voice like your brother’s says he needs urgent financial help. The number is unfamiliar. Each decision is a fresh start; what you did or paid in one does not carry into the next.

steps.prompt: He asks you to stay on the line while a “lawyer” explains how to pay.

choices.text: End this call and ring his saved number.
choices.consequence: You leave room for an independent check.
choices.explanation: The “lawyer” was chosen by the caller and cannot vouch for the caller.

choices.text: Hear the lawyer out, as a form of verification.
choices.consequence: A second actor adds to the pressure.
choices.explanation: Two voices on a call the scammer controls are still one source.

steps.prompt: A fresh start: you hang up the incoming call and dial your brother’s saved number. Nobody answers. What next?

choices.consequence: The attacker gets the money, and may ask for more.
choices.explanation: A test payment is still money sent to someone you have not verified.

choices.text: Try another relative, or an institution at a published number.
choices.consequence: You look for independent word of how he is.
choices.explanation: Silence from your brother does not make the caller’s payment story true.

steps.prompt: A fresh start: no money has gone. A caller with a voice like your brother’s knows your family phrase and asks for a transfer. Do you pay?

choices.text: Wait for independent confirmation of the person and the request.
choices.consequence: The phrase counts as one clue, not as permission to pay.
choices.explanation: A shared phrase can leak or be coaxed out of someone; check through a saved route.

choices.text: Pay: only the family knows that phrase.
choices.consequence: In this exercise the payment goes to an unverified recipient.
choices.explanation: Knowing a phrase is not independent confirmation.

blocks.debrief: Urgency did not make the check optional. When a real emergency is plausible, look for help through institutions you can verify, and hold back any unverified payment. Replay any step to practise.

questions.prompt: A manager’s familiar voice asks you to change a supplier’s bank details. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Approve it, because you recognise the voice.
choices.explanation: Cloning and ordinary impersonation both mean a voice alone proves nothing.

choices.text: Follow the documented payment-change and callback process.
choices.explanation: Financial controls apply whatever the voice sounds like.

questions.prompt: A caller knows a private childhood detail. Does that settle who they are?

choices.text: No; the detail may have leaked or been researched.
choices.explanation: A question about what someone knows is weaker than a route you choose yourself.

choices.text: Yes; a clone cannot know facts.
choices.explanation: The person behind a clone can look the facts up and work them into the call.

questions.prompt: The real person cannot be reached, but the danger may be genuine. What now?

choices.text: Ignore every emergency until the person rings back.
choices.explanation: A real emergency may need a quick call to a reliable institution.

choices.text: Contact another trusted person or the local emergency service, and make no unverified payment.
choices.explanation: You can check on someone’s welfare quickly without accepting the caller’s payment channel.
